title: Automating detection of Two-Level Systems in Superconducting Qubits
authors: Rama Khalil, Cameron J. Kopas, Avinash Pathapati, Rory Cochrane, Xiqiao Wang, Hossein Taghinejad, Vito Iaia, Josh Mutus, Yaniv J. Rosen, Jared H. Cole, David P. Pappas, Alexander V. Balatsky
abstract: Microscopic two-level system (TLS) defects remain a primary mechanism of decoherence and operational instability in superconducting transmon qubits, necessitating scalable and automated methods for their characterization. Here, we present and benchmark two complementary analysis pipelines for extracting TLS statistics directly from time-resolved SWAP spectroscopy: one-dimensional decay-rate fitting (1D-DRF), which detects defects via localized enhancements in the qubit relaxation rate, and a deterministic, non-parametric computer-vision framework (2D-CV) that achieves two-dimensional spectral localization by exploiting the temporal persistence of coherent population suppression. We deploy both methods on SWAP spectroscopy measurements from 52 flux-tunable transmon qubits on Rigetti processors with and without moderate ($\sim 10\%$) post-fabrication frequency trimming via Alternating-Bias Assisted Annealing (ABAA). We show that both pipelines converge on a consistent global characterization of the defect landscape while exhibiting complementary sensitivity across distinct coupling regimes. Crucially, both methods independently reveal a count--loss decoupling under moderate annealing: while the total detectable TLS defect density remains statistically unchanged, the span-integrated dielectric loss is reduced by approximately a factor of two, demonstrating selective suppression of the most strongly dissipative defect channels. These results establish an automated, non-parametric analysis framework for high-throughput hardware diagnostics and provide a statistical baseline for post-fabrication defect engineering in large-scale superconducting quantum processors.
summary: This work presents and benchmarks two advanced, automated methods for detecting TLS defects in superconducting transmon qubits using SWAP spectroscopy. The authors show that by applying a moderate annealing process, they can selectively suppress the most damaging defect channels, significantly reducing energy loss without altering the total number of defects. This establishes a robust diagnostic tool for improving large-scale quantum hardware.
main_problem: Microscopic Two-Level System (TLS) defects are a primary source of decoherence and instability in superconducting transmon qubits, necessitating scalable and automated characterization methods.
main_result: The study demonstrates a count–loss decoupling effect where post-fabrication annealing selectively suppresses the strongest dissipative defect channels, halving the integrated loss without changing the total defect count.
method: Two complementary analysis pipelines—1D decay-rate fitting (1D-DRF) and a deterministic 2D computer-vision framework (2D-CV)—are benchmarked to extract TLS statistics from time-resolved SWAP spectroscopy maps.
model_or_system: The system involves flux-tunable transmon qubits on Rigetti processors, modeled by a Hamiltonian including coupling to TLS defects. Measurements utilize SWAP spectroscopy to map qubit population decay across time and frequency.
key_observables: TLS defect density, localized resonant loss ($\Gamma_{TLS}$), frequency-integrated TLS loss strength ($I_{TLS}$), and qubit relaxation rates ($T_1$).
important_parameters: Moderate post-fabrication annealing ($\sim 10\%$) is the key intervention; the analysis compares results across different junction geometries.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed loss reduction is due to the annealing treatment modifying barrier coordination, rather than being an artifact of sample allocation.
figures_summary: Figures compare the performance of 1D vs. 2D analysis pipelines, showing how the 2D method captures weakly dissipative structures, and illustrate the systematic depletion of high-dissipation defects after annealing.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the two distinct analysis pipelines (1D-DRF and 2D-CV), applies both to experimental data (with and without annealing), and concludes by comparing the quantitative results and interpreting the physical meaning of the observed loss reduction.
why_interesting: The development of a non-parametric, automated analysis framework (2D-CV) for extracting subtle decoherence signatures from complex 2D spectroscopic data is highly valuable for characterizing open quantum systems.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
